findings.evidence: Wrenford "bega" = three: misheard: biga → bega (generation 23) · Oakhollow "bega" = three: misheard: biga → bega (generation 23) · Ironcrag "thedu" = no: misheard: thidu → thedu (generation 12)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.52, p = 0.094, n = 12. Most used: two (13% replaced per generation), wood (21% replaced per generation), food (10% replaced per generation); least: planks (49%), five (69%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: 2 founding families still alive. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.65, p = <0.001, n = 25.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
